title: Young stellar jet MHO 2147
caption: The young stellar jet MHO 2147, imaged by the Gemini South telescope
credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA · Acknowledgments: Image processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab) · PI: L. Ferrero (Universidad Nacional de Córdoba)

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: A sinuous jet of gas drifts lazily across a star field in this infrared image of MHO 2147, captured from Chile with the Gemini South telescope. The jet is an outflow from a young star hidden inside an infrared dark cloud, in the direction of Sagittarius.

Young stars often launch narrow jets while they are still growing, driving material away as gas continues to fall onto them. The jet of MHO 2147 does not run straight, though: it snakes from side to side. Astronomers suspect this sidewinding shape is caused by the gravitational pull of companion stars, which would tug the young star and swing the direction of its jet.

The crisp detail comes from Gemini South's adaptive optics system, which lets astronomers undo much of the blurring caused by turbulence in Earth's atmosphere. Infrared light also passes through dust more easily than visible light, which helps astronomers study young objects buried in dusty clouds.

understand.summary: A near-infrared image from the GSAOI instrument on Gemini South, using adaptive optics, through a molecular hydrogen (H2) filter and a broadband filter; the colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, so the colours here are a translation of light we cannot see.
